title: Lexeme Fragment Coordinator and Onboard Compatibility Probe
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: During model onboarding we repeatedly see subtle mismatches between the model's subword segmentation heuristics and the chat template delimiters used by our runtime. These mismatches lead to off-by-one token counts, role boundary leakage, degraded caching efficiency, and in a few customer cases, unexpected regression in output quality after pinning a model variant.

Goal: Implement a Lexeme Fragment Coordinator (LFC) — a runtime-side preflight and runtime shim that detects, normalizes, and reports lexeme-fragment (subword) boundary mismatches between incoming chat templates and the model's tokenizer rules during onboarding and canary rollouts; wire its signals into the performance profile publishing pipeline so onboarding decisions (pin, profile publish, fallback) are aware of tokenization friction.

Scope and Acceptance Criteria:
- Add LFC component that: 1) runs a lightweight preflight tokenization pass using the model bundle's tokenizer; 2) compares segmentation against canonical chat template framing rules; 3) classifies mismatch types (delimiter loss, span-split, subtoken-escape) and computes a mismatch rate metric.
- Expose LFC telemetry into onboarding dashboards: per-model mismatch_rate, mismatch_type_breakdown, avg_extra_tokens, and downstream cache hit ratio delta.
- Add safety checks to onboarding pipeline: if mismatch_rate > 0.5% for prompts > 200 tokens or > 2.0% for prompts < 200 tokens, then flag automated pinning for human review and do not publish perf profile until addressed.
- Implement a runtime fallback that coerces delimiter framing only for pinned canaries (configurable via onboard config) and ensure KV cache key stability is preserved when coercion is enabled.
- Add unit and integration tests: deterministic tokenizer roundtrip tests, synthetic prompts exercising edge delimiters, and canary rollout smoke.
- Update performance profile publishing job to include a lexeme_compatibility section summarizing LFC findings.

Implementation Plan:
1) Prototype LFC as a standalone binary integrated into onboarding harness (risk-limited): add instrumentation to call LFC during onboarding runs and record metrics to the onboarding namespace.
2) Build a normalization library that contains framing heuristics and conservative fixes (e.g., explicit role markers escaping, stable delimiter substitution). Keep heuristics pluggable per model family.
3) Wire coaching signals into the publishing workflow: gating rules, human review flag, and an opt-in automatic coercion for low-risk models.
4) Add regression tests and a canary with 3 customers in Dedicated and 2 private deployments where we can toggle coercion at the route level for testing.

Risks and Mitigations:
- False positives in mismatch detection could block legitimate models: mitigate by validating on a large corpus of historical prompts and exposing a manual override in the console.
- Coercion may change user-visible outputs: limit coercion to canary/pinned routes only and compare against baseline in canary metrics.
- KV cache key divergence when coercion enabled: design coercion to be KV-stable (record canonicalized key variant) and add a cache-compatibility test harness.

Monitoring and Rollback:
- Dashboard alerts when mismatch_rate spikes > 3x baseline during onboarding or after profile publish.
- Automated rollback path: when canary metric delta for semantic-similarity drops by > 5% or customer error reports spike, immediately un-publish the perf profile and revert coercion.

Outcomes and Follow-ups:
- Short term: reduce onboarding surprises and lower manual effort for model pinning decisions by surfacing quantifiable lexeme incompatibility signals.
- Medium term: integrate LFC into runtime for live request-time light normalization where safe, and incorporate lexeme_compatibility into SLA scoring for Dedicated customers.

Notes for reviewers: pay attention to the gating thresholds and canary test selection. The first iteration intentionally errs on the side of human review rather than automatic changes.
